rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi identifies the Qur’anic allusion as Psalm 37, whose discrete stanzas pair counsel with a repeated promise that the pious inherit the land.
rows.anchor: discrete stanzas in which words of counsel are sounded first and then a repetitive verse occurs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised inheritance cannot mean the present earth: it is mortal, and God gives respite there to both righteous and wicked people.
rows.anchor: this earth and all of its things are mortal and God has given respite in it to both the righteous and the wicked

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Psalm’s eternal inheritance concerns the Hereafter: the present sky and earth will be destroyed and replaced by a new world for the righteous, as Qur’an 21:104 and 14:48 indicate.
rows.anchor: Earlier in verse 104, it is pointed out that one day the Almighty will destroy this sky.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The new earth and sky will belong eternally to the righteous; wrongdoers will have no share and will be cast into Hell.
rows.anchor: they will eternally belong to the righteous. The wrongdoers will have no share in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi notes that the Psalms are hymns revealed to David, a prophet and illustrious king, making his proclamation of the final righteous kingdom especially forceful.
rows.anchor: a prophet as well as an illustrious king.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic allusion recalls the Psalm’s moving elaboration and repeated promise, preceded by counsel; Islahi says this counsel guarantees the eternal kingdom in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: it is these words of counsel which guarantee an eternal kingdom in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word balāgh encompasses general declaration and glad tidings; its indefinite form magnifies the verdict that only righteous servants inherit the new earth and urges worshippers to strive for the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The word ﻎﺑَﻠٰـ here encompasses the meanings of general declaration and general glad tidings. It is undefined to magnify it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sent the Prophet as mercy to deliver glad tidings and warnings; his duty is proclamation, and he should tell mockers that he brings mercy rather than punishment and does not know its timing.
rows.anchor: God has sent the Prophet (sws) as a mercy for mankind to deliver glad tidings and warnings to people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse ends with a forceful warning to submit to the powerful, everlasting God; the Prophet has discharged his duty, so persistent opponents bear the consequences themselves.
rows.anchor: The last part of the verse carries a vehement warning: are these people willing to consign themselves to the powerful and ever-existing God or not?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If they still evade the decisive warning, the Prophet should say that leaders and followers, rich and poor, were all warned equally and that only God knows when the danger will arrive.
rows.anchor: he has informed their leaders and their followers, the prominent and the ordinary, the rich and the poor all about the imminent danger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God knows both hidden and public aspects of people’s lives, they should entrust their affair to Him; He knows their demand and its motive.
rows.anchor: when God knows the hidden and the known aspects of peoples’ lives, they should consign their matter to him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents demanded punishment to provoke the Prophet and deceive the masses, not from sincere belief; God knows their secrets, so the Prophet trusts His knowledge and wisdom.
rows.anchor: They only did so to annoy and pester him and to deceive their masses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in laʿallahu refers to the delayed promise; its delay may test them until proof is complete or give them respite, so they should repent in the first case and be grateful in the second.
rows.anchor: is the “delayed promise” indicated in the previous verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s closing prayer is also a farewell to his enemies: he seeks God’s judgment and help concerning their words and deeds, and Islahi says God accepted the supplication.
rows.anchor: This verse is both a supplication from the Prophet (sws) and also a farewell to the enemies.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These words complete the sūrah’s explanation, followed by praise to God.
rows.anchor: With these words, the explanation of this sū rah comes to its completion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi dates Sūrah al-Ḥajj to the late Makkan period, when persecution was forcing Muslims to migrate and the Prophet’s migration was near.
rows.anchor: This sūrah is among the last of the Makkan ones revealed when Muslims were being forced to migrate to other areas

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah warns Quraysh of God’s wrath, argues for monotheism and resurrection, and uses Abraham’s preaching and the House’s purpose to establish Muslims as its rightful custodians.
rows.anchor: They are warned of God’s wrath, and monotheism and the certainty of the Day of Judgement is corroborated through convincing arguments.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conquest of Makkah, hinted at in 21:44, becomes a decisive verdict here: Quraysh are usurpers threatened with expulsion, while Muslims are promised protection and custody of the House.
rows.anchor: The conquest of Makkah has been hinted in verse 44 of the previous sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only verses 38–41 were revealed in Madinah; they permit Muslims to fight defensively if Quraysh block Hajj, since the Muslims are the House’s rightful custodians.
rows.anchor: In these verses, Muslims are permitted to take up arms in defence if the disbelievers of the Quraysh try to forcibly stop them from doing ḥajj.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although exegetes dispute the sūrah’s place of revelation because of those verses, Islahi holds that a few explanatory Madinan verses do not make the whole sūrah Madinan, as with Sūrah al-Muzzammil.
rows.anchor: then this does not make the whole sūrah into a Madīnan one.

none: The segment contains translated Qur’anic text only.
